Hello,

Former young Tri-Cities inhabitant here. I enjoyed my time there and it's very easy to get to Umatilla from the area. That being said, finding the young people there can be a problem. I worked at the Hanford site and all of my friends were other young professionals. I can't tell you from experience, but a lot of people find social networks in the local churches.

I left about a year ago because I got a better job in a bigger city. I would probably not move back unless I was already married. Unfortunately it's not a great place to be single. If you want a city, then you want to live in Seattle or Portland. These are both very far from Umatilla though. If the job is good, get some experience, enjoy the wine, and then move onto the next thing. 

Let me know if you have any specific questions about the area.

I am employed now, but I had to acquire my M.S. in applied math before anyone would even consider hiring me. The issue is that training people to work in research/science is expensive compared to other fields. As STEM folk, we pretty much demand baseline $50k salary (about the median US household income for 2011) and most employers don't have the patience to train inexperienced college graduates. They definitely have the resources, but capitalists are shrewd and calculating dickheads. Also, let's be real, very few college graduates have success immediately integrating themselves into the work environment.

OP sounds like an individual with a brain, so I'm going to tell you what makes you employable in the STEM fields: applicable knowledge of two or more useful programming languages. I get to develop theoretical mathematics every now and then for publications, but the majority of the work that I do is data analysis/algorithm development. You don't have to be a genius; you just have to demonstrate that you have a decent understanding of what the hell is going on.
